 The large field of creative writing splits into subcategories (fiction, poetry, creative-nonfiction) and there are even specialized genres (sci-fi, mysteries, experimental… the list goes on). Figure out what you want to write. Write what you would want to read. Your best writing will spring forth from something that you, and maybe only you, are passionate about. When your passion is injected into your writing, your readers will, in turn, be interested. Your passion for your individual writing project is a powerful tool that will serve well as a starting point.


Remember that you don’t have to limit yourself to a single field. Many established writers spread out and explore—perhaps they write creative essays while publishing their creative non-fiction work. Maybe their short novels have poems inside of them.;
, Establish a particular time of day, location, and atmosphere for your writing sessions. As you establish this routine, the creative side of your brain will become accustomed to working in these familiar conditions. Things to consider are…


Noise: some writers enjoy absolute quiet. Others will listen to music to jog their creative juices. Others will want the company of friends to bounce ideas.
Time: Some writers jot down thoughts just before they sleep. Early mornings hours work well for others, as fewer people are awake to bother them. Other writers may enjoy being badgered, and therefore write in between coffee break or other work sessions. Other writers will like long periods of undisturbed writing time, and dedicate their weekends to writing.
Location: establishing a particular building, room, or even chair can help the writing process. This familiarity will train your brain to work creatively, or technically, to suit your goals.

, Reread the things you have enjoyed and study them—figure out what makes them effective, what makes them work. Try to understand the structure of your favorite poem, or the evolution of the characters in your favorite novel. Find a sentence that you think is great, and wonder—why did that author choose that phrase? This word?


Do not limit yourself single genres or fields. To truly enrich your writing experience, you must explore. You may not enjoy fantasy, but other people read and write fantasy for a reason. Read with this motto in mind: “I read to write. I read to learn. I read to be inspired.”

, Notice things. Pay attention to the world around you. Look for mysteries and try to solve them. If you have questions, pursue the answers with obsessive interest. Take special note of the quirky and unusual. When writing, having noticed things will help give you something to write about. Moreover, it can help make your writing more compelling, richer, and more realistic. Here are some pointers that will help you explore the world around you:


Nothing is ordinary or boring. There’s something odd or special about everyone and everything.
There’s a mystery in front of you: a TV that won’t turn on, a bird that won’t fly. Figure out how things work, don’t work, and why.
Pay attention to detail. The leaves are not only green: they've got long, thin veins, rigid stems, and are shaped like spades.

, Write down things that you notice or that inspire you. Take it everywhere you go. Some famous writers even went as far as to sew extra pockets into their jackets in order to carry more scraps of paper. Use this journal to produce ideas, take note of things you see, hear, or read, and flesh out your writing material. When you get stuck on your project, you can revisit it for inspiration. Understand that everything can go in your notebook, because everything is a source of inspiration. Some useful things are:


Dreams: a major source of the weird and unusual. Write it down before it disappears!
Pictures: photographs and doodles
Quotes: things people say, sentences that surprise you, short poems, the insides of a fortune cookie

, This is the most important part, and it can be very hard. Many of us stare blankly at the computer screen, with no words to write. Some call it “writers block.” To help, here are some basic writing exercises that can help jog your creative juices and provide a material for your project:


Go somewhere busy, preferably a place with lots of people. Imagine that your vision of the scene is a video camera, recording everything. Take out your notebook and write down exactly what is happening. Include all the senses—sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch.
Take a voice recorder, and spy on a conversation. Don’t let the speakers know! After you've recorded for an adequate amount of time, transcribe the conversation on paper. Play with the words—delete things, change things, add things. Create a new setting, or a new situation.
Create a character. What do they want? Fear? What is their secret? Who are they related to, and where do they live? What’s their last name…if they even have one?

, There are a billion half-novels in the world and a trillion half-short stories. Setting a goal and sticking to it, however unpleasant the work gets, is essential to figuring out what you want to write. By the time you finish whatever you set out to write in the first place, you’ll have three things:

a good idea what you really want to write about
some skill with which to write about it
the tenacity to finish the job

, Sharing ideas and getting feedback is one of the best ways to become inspired and to improve your work. This can be scary for beginner writers, for your work can be something incredibly personal, and you may be afraid of rejection. However, writing in isolation means that not only is no one reading your work, but you can also run the risk of compounding bad habits (being too wordy, redundant, or melodramatic, etc.). Instead of being scared, think that every person you share your work with is a potential person to give you new ideas and inspire you.

, Being a writer is almost like being a superhero: awkward office job by day… dragon-riding, super sleuth, knight in armor WRITER by night. Some creative writers do not have day jobs—but this is very rare. However, having a day job is not a bad thing. In fact, a good day job can even be helpful to your goal in becoming a writer. When finding your dream day job, here are some things to consider:


Does it pay the bills? A good day job should ease your financial burdens so you can write without worry. Stress is not conducive to your project.
Does it leave you enough time and energy to write? A good day job should be easy enough on your energy level so that you’re not exhausted afterwards.
Does it provide a good “distraction”? Having a space away from your writing work can be helpful. Spending too much time on a single project can be overly immersive. It is good to take a step back.
Does it have other creative people? A good day job should give you awesome coworkers. Creative people are everywhere! They are not just writers or artists.

, No, don’t literally put them in handcuffs! Immerse them in your work. Suck them into the writing so that they will read and read and never want to escape, so that they will want you to handcuff them to your next book. To do this, here are some techniques you can use:


The senses. We perceive and experience the world through our senses. An immersive and convincing work will often have readers seeing, touching, tasting, hearing, and smelling.
Concrete details. These types of details provide a specific sense of understanding of what is going on in the writing. Rather than generalizing an image—“she was pretty”—get specific: “She had long, golden braids, which were interwoven with daisies.”

, If you are more familiar with something, you can write about it in more detail, realism, and depth. If you don’t know a detail that is important for your project, do research. Google it. Ask someone who knows. The more information you know about a situation, a person, or setting, the more you will be able to render it realistically on the page.

, Sometimes, the best way to write a story is “Linear Structure”: Beginning, Climax, and Resolution. However, there are many, many other ways to write a story. Consider “In Media Res”—when the story begins in the thick of things. Or, a story interspersed by multiple flashbacks. Choose your structure depending on your story’s progression.

, The 3 main categories are 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Person. When deciding point of view, think about what information you want your readers to have access to.


1st POV: uses "I"

involved – narrator is an active player and teller of the story
detached – narrator is not telling their own story specifically, but maybe the story of a central character
Plural (we) – a collective narrator, maybe a large group of people


2nd POV: uses "You"

inverted, the narrator is referring to him or herself as the writer, and perhaps dissociating themselves from distasteful thoughts/traits/memories
You = a character, distinct with their own unique qualities
You = direct address to the reader
You = reader is active character in the story


3rd POV: uses a character name

omniscient – narrator knows everything, has free reign in the story and complete authority, and can hurl judgments
limited – this POV is missing something. It is like a window of vision that gets smaller and smaller as you become more limited
single characters’ thoughts and feelings -- Harry Potter is limited to Harry's thoughts and feelings
direct observer -- a narrator's telling of situation, but cannot explicitly discern the emotions of the characters
fly on the wall--the narrator is spy, watching the situation from a distant perspective, but is not privy to everything for information is limited by the narrator's location on the wall



, Simple is the best way to start. While you will undoubtedly need a well-stocked vocabulary (more on that later), too many big words will drive all but the most dedicated readers away. Start small. Don't hold onto a grandiose word just because it sounds fancy. Aim instead to allow everyone who reads your writing to comprehend exactly what you wanted them to comprehend. Nothing more, and nothing less.

, Short sentences are easy to digest and are very readable. That's not to say that you can't, or shouldn't, write a long sentence every once in a while. It's just that simple sentences deliver information without stopping the reader in his or her tracks, stranding them on an island of befuddlement.


Take a look at a notorious long, overwrought sentence. The following sentence won the satirical Bad Writing Contest second-prize. It's no secret why it qualifies as "bad writing." The sentence is caked in jargon, riddled with imprecise catchphrases, and is way too long:

"If, for a while, the ruse of desire is calculable for the uses of discipline soon the repetition of guilt, justification, pseudo-scientific theories, superstition, spurious authorities, and classifications can be seen as the desperate effort to “normalize” formally the disturbance of a discourse of splitting that violates the rational, enlightened claims of its enunciatory modality.", Verbs are the great drivers of sentences. They carry meaning from one thought to the next. On top of that, they help writers achieve dazzling degrees of precision.


Pay close attention to certain problem verbs. Verbs such as "did," "went," "saw," "felt," and "had," while occasionally appropriate, don't really add any spice to your writing. Substitute a more specific word for problem verbs when appropriate: "accomplished," "skipped," "gazed," "experienced," and "secure" all communicate more specific ideas.
Use the active voice instead of the passive voice, as a rule of thumb.
Active voice: "The cat found her master." Here, the cat is doing the work, so to speak. She is actively finding her master.
Passive voice: "The master is found by his cat." Here, the cat is more removed from the action. The master is being found; the cat isn't finding.



, The beginning writer will go crazy with adjectives. There's nothing wrong with adjectives, except that they can sometimes be redundant and are often more obscure — and therefore harder to understand — than other parts of speech. Don't feel like you need to include an adjective before every noun in order to describe the noun.


Sometimes, adjectives are redundant. Take the sentence "I watched as he lifted the last pawn and set it down, checkmating the king, clinching his successful victory." What victory isn't successful? Here, the adjective simply restates what we already know. It doesn't add anything to to help the reader comprehend what's going on.
Other times, the adjectives writers use can be pretty obscure. "He is a puissant adversary" is a sentence that is neither accessible nor fitting. "Puissant" means powerful, and substituting "powerful" for "puissant" would have made the sentence both understandable and bearable.

, Keep a dictionary and thesaurus by your side at all times. Whenever you come across a word that you don't know, look it up. It's hard to call yourself a writer if you're not at least marginally interested in etymology. At the same time, use your vocabulary sparingly. Just because you know the words "defenestrate," "pyknic," and "agnomen" doesn't mean you should be finding excuses to use them.


Study roots of words. Word roots (especially Latin roots for the English language) will help you decipher the meanings of unknown words without a dictionary. Knowing the roots mal-, ben-, epi-, eu-, ag-, and con- is a good start.

, It's tempting for people who use words for a living to use them a little loosely. Often, when we're stuck and we don't know which word to use, we wing it and write down a word that's "good enough." This strategy is useful and necessary in everyday conversation, but problematic in writing.


For one, there's no social context. The writer can't use his or her hands to gesture, and can't rely on facial expressions to steer the conversation toward clarity. The reader is all alone, and must rely solely on the words to gather meaning.
Second, the reader takes what the writer says at face value. The reader doesn't expect to have to ask the writer whether she meant what she wrote; the reader assumes that the writer meant what she wrote. The writer doesn't clarify confusing words, which means that if you write down a confusing word, the reader is left confused.

For these reasons, take the time to say what you mean. Figure out what you want to say before you say it. Be dogged about sniffing out the right word, even if it takes you time. A lot of sub-par writing is the refusal to fit the right word with an idea, not issues with plot or stylistic concerns.

, Examples of figurative language are metaphor and simile. It's best to use metaphor and simile when you want to dramatize or draw the reader's attention to something specific. Like saying "I love you," figurative language loses much of its power if used incessantly.

, Good punctuation is neither seen nor heard, but is powerful nonetheless. Underuse punctuation and your readers won't be able to understand the meaning of your sentences. "Let's eat, Mommy," and "Let's eat Mommy" have two very different meanings. Overuse punctuation and your readers will be distracted. No one wants to read a sentence in which colons, semicolons, and dashes make more appearances that actual words.


Exclamation points. Use exclamation points sparingly. People don't often exclaim things; nor do sentences often merit exclamation. Elmore Leonard, the great crime writer, has this to say: "Keep your exclamation points under control. You are allowed no more than two or three per 100,000 words of prose."
Semicolons. Semicolons act as hybrid periods, connecting two sentences that have logical connection. Still, Kurt Vonnegut argues against them: "Do not use semicolons. They are transvestite hermaphrodites representing absolutely nothing. All they do is show you've been to college."Although Vonnegut's assessment might be a little harsh, it's probably only good to use them from time to time.

, Don't be afraid to invert rules or play with them to achieve the sort of writing you want. Some of the greatest writers have successfully broken grammatical, stylistic, and semantic rules, making literature better by doing so. Know why you're breaking the rule in the first place, and understand its likely effect. But if you're not willing to take some risks, what are you doing calling yourself a writer?

 
[Text End]

prompt_text:
You're a professional wordsmith. Summarize the following blog article into a concise summary, ensuring that all essential information is included. 
[Text Start]: 
I want to begin by saying I'm a long time supporter of Samsung and their products. From TV's, washing machines, dishwashers, fridges, cords,headsets, and phones I have always stood by them. I am a registered Platinum Member in fact and I just want to make it clear I'm not bashing them in anyway and think they are handling this as best as they can however it is quite a shit show. 
 (Feel free to go down to the exchange heading if you are only interested in that however I'd appreciate your time) 
 
 Purchasing 
 
 I purchased the phone day 2 in store (using Tmobiles old jump program as Im grandfathered into it) and was told it was gonna be mailed as it was out of stock in store. I had travel planned at the end of the coming week and wanted to have the phone for it. In the store I was told 4 business days tops and since it was a Friday and I wasn't leaving until the following Friday that I'd be fine. Trusting in this I opted against going and buying it outright somewhere else and having to deal with activating it. I checked my Tmobile account daily starting Saturday where I saw it said my note 5 was my "trade device" and then there was just nothing under the "new device" tab. I wasn't concerned figuring it had just went through no big deal. Sunday- nothing no change. Monday-no change and I was at this point figuring the site must have a bug and just not show it. Now I waited until Wednesday to check again seeing then that still no progress had been made. I had received an email the day prior with a tracking number but when I looked it up USPS said nothing was found. So now Thursday morning I decide that there must be a problem as nothing had changed. 
 So I call in and the rep asks me for my account info and upon pulling it up she too cant see anything for my new device. She is apologetic but after 15minutes of her trying to get into the account she gives up and says she'll need her supervisor. I wait another 10 minutes and she comes back and says she still wasnt able to totally open the account however she can track it and says its at my local post office and out to be delivered. Great! I thank her and hangup. Where I live they don't deliver mail so when mail is being delivered it just means they are sorting it to your box so I head down to the post office.  I know the postman well and he says he hasn't got anything for me and checks the whole data base and nothing comes up.  So now I'm showing him the tracking number in the email tmobile sent me and he immediately sees that for whatever reason they doubled the numbers up and thats why it wasnt working so he checks the number and is able to tell me that not only have they not shipped it but not even gave it to USPS all they have done it print a label. So I return home and call again to find out why they told me it was shipped. The gentlemen I speak with tells me he's sorry and has no idea where this other agent got this info from. On top of that he's sorry to say that it wont probably ship for a few days still as its back ordered. I ask why no one told me and just get more sorrys. So fast forward to 3 days later I return and finally have the device. 
 
 Ownership 
 
 Now once I got it I had a little problem transferring my old data using the included connector and cord. Ended up using the old wireless system and synced quickly. Now I had no problems from here on out other than I noticed it got quite warm but I use fast charge battery packs as I'm on the go often so whatever I think nothing of it as my note 3 got warm way back when it had just came out. 
 Fast forward to D-Day its top news every where that note 7's are bursting into flames. Shit. So I now begin to only charge while I'm watching it and in a metal bin whatever not a big deal however whats the plan what am I to do with the other 2 million people. 
 I get that answer days later when a message is given that all retailers are gonna be issuing some sort of return process and give a loaner phone. Eh well okay at least they are taking care of me. Well not really days go by and I hear what some carriers are doing but nothing from T-Mobile hell not even an email from them that I have a recalled piece of equipment that is a possible hazard to my health. 
 Finally I get an email from them that says I have 3 options. 1.sign up to be told when the new phone is ready 2.Switch to a new device totally forever or 3.Return for full refund 
 I call in to see if I can exchange like I heard other carriers are doing for just a loaner phone. I'm given a resounding NO that I'd be at that point choosing option 3 and returning and that I'd be getting the loaner phone on my own dime and I could just hope that within the 14 day return period that I'd be able to get a new note 7. Ha no way. I'll just be careful with the phone. Now almost a week passes and I got the text from yesterday saying that now they are really gonna take care of me. This is quotation directly from the page..... 
 "We’re making it easy for you to exchange your Galaxy Note7 for free. 
 Just head into one of our retail stores to exchange your device. We’ll take care of the rest. Or you can call us today at 1-844-275-9309. We’ll ship you any device of your choice in our inventory with free next business day shipping. You can keep it or use it as a “loaner” until the new Note7 is available." 
 If it looks to good to be true... 
 
 Exchange 
 
 So after my past experiences there is no way in hell I'm calling in when I'm given the option to handle this in the store as they tend to be a lot more accountable when we are face to face. So I go in and have a group ahead of me in line browsing the store so I sit down on the side and wait. The female rep asks if anyone is here to pay a bill or anything like that, that'll be quick I say yeah I'm just here to exchange for my loaner phone from the note 7 program. She is visibly displeased and lets me know that its a 30 minute process. I say okay thats fine I can wait to which she says well the last one took 45 minutes I say okay thats still fine I can wait. 15 minutes pass and a manager comes from the back letting me know I need to just call in to handle this as the store isnt capable and hands me a paper with the number written down. I let him know that the message I received from T-Mobile said quite the opposite to which he says there is no way he can exchange it in store as the hotline has the only system that allows the process and tells me he's sorry but over the past few days they tried to do it in store and simply couldn't as they don't even have the stock of s7/s7 edges to give out loaner phones. 
 I finish my errands return home and immediately call and get quickly connected to Amy. Amy is quite chipper and lets me know the process is quite simple and all I need to do is head in the store and I'll be taken care of with an exchange loaner device of my choice. I laugh and let her know what I was told and she becomes concerned and says there is no way that could have happened as, as soon as the store sees a note 7 they are too immediately exchange  for any device even if all they have is Iphones as its considered a liability and safety concern. So I tell her then please note this information exactly on my account and I'll head back in. She notes it all with policy numbers even and I drive back. 
 Upon arriving the store is armed with different employees from earlier except the female rep running the counter. She immediately goes in the back bringing a new manager who asks me, "How can I help you?" I tell him the situation and how I was already here and he says that the number I was given is the only thing he can do to help me. I explain that this is not the case and that I have notes on my account that should explain it clearly. He checks and says that this is old information and is not what his District Officer advised him on. He offers I call from the store phone and just try again. I oblige and speak with John. John tells me within 30 seconds that I can just head into a store to get my loaner. I ask him if he could hold for just one moment and tell that to the T-Mobile manager sitting across from me. They now I kid you not go back and forth for 15minutes telling each other different policys and how each other are wrong. I'm nearly laughing at the ridiculousness of the situation as 2 reps of the same company tell each they don't know policy. He eventually hangs up and tells me he is sorry but these guys on the phone don't know what they are talking about as there "system doesn't just have a magic loaner button". I tell him I understand but what am I to do as I'm just getting the run around no matter what I do. He says the main problem is, that my note 7 when I got it had a tax charge as all things do when they leave the store. He says that there is no way for me to get a tax charge in there system therefore he cant give me anything as thatd be illegal. I tell him that I understand the predicament but uhh what do I do? He then tells me he's gonna try a few things with his other employee. They spend 20 minutes and get no where. He then says he is trying to contact the District Officer or someone higher up but it could take a while. Sure why not I can wait. 45 minutes go by and still nothing. Now they are just trying different things in the system and finally come up with a way to get me a new device. However its gonna use an upgrade and also is outside the "hotline loaner program" therefore I'm now not entitled to a note 7 when they come out but he says he can make it note but its not legally binding and he cant promise anything. Yeah no way so he says just try and call in again tonight. 
 I leave defeated and as I'm driving home I pass Verizon. Out of curiosity I pull over and look up the location and call them. I speak with John and ask him what is the process for the note 7 debacle. He is very friendly and says that for now all his location is doing is giving full refunds and thats it. I come clean and tell him I'm not with Verizon but T-Mobile and tell him my situation. He asks which location did I go too. I tell him and sure enough he says he used to work there and that they are know as the "idiots of the district who always call in and end up just throwing there hands in the air and give up" Wow great. He then in detail explains to me what they should have done in the system as he knows it well when he worked there and I tell him the problem with taxes to which he replies should be a non problem as when they refund the first note 7 I should get a credit for the original tax. Nevertheless he tells me to go to this other T-Mobile location he was at and gives me employee names to speak with. I thank him and return home. 
 Now I decide I'll attempt this hotline one final time. Dana picks up and listens to it all and says she is sorry I'm going through this and can't believe the disconnect from the stores and hotline. She though is able to actually send me a loaner over the phone and works with me to get all the info. She asks what phone I want to which I decide why not try an Iphone 6s+ as I havent had an Iphone since the original 5. So she confirms it all and I think back to a problem I've had in the past when I moved a few months ago. There was a wrong street number which I had called and had "fixed" twice in the past so I ask her what address she is sending to and of course its wrong. Jesus Christ, I tell her its wrong and she corrects it and the call concludes telling me to sign my EIP when it comes to my email. 
 FINALLY this nightmare is over.... right? Well 2 hours pass and I get the email and sign it. And its now almost midnight, what a day. I get the final confirmation email and read it over. Yep you know it guess what was wrong??? The address. Still. Wrong. 
 (I actually started writing this post at this point but got even more content to write lol) 
I'm now finally at my wits end, I've kept calm all day and been very understanding but now I'm pretty sure I'm gonna have a heart attack. I call its 12:02am and I speak with Ieasha who hears a very abbreviated gloss over the situation to which I tell her I just need the address fixed on my current shipment. Guess what no she cant. Once the EIP is signed it cant be canceled. She tries for 20minutes and has me explain the whole situation. She then says shes gonna have me talk to a supervisor who she has explained how crazy this has gotten. 
 Kendall the head supervisor is now talking to me who says she is gonna put this to bed no matter what it takes right here and now. I tell her that this is my last call to T-Mobile as otherwise I will be going in and demanding full refunds and canceling my 5 year long account with them. I let her know the entire problem and go into detail with the exact disconnects I see between the stores and hotline. I tell her about how I had them even arguing over the phone on what policy was. I conclude the story with telling her that as the customer I have done my due diligence and that this is in her hands to get higher ups to hopefully fix this nightmare of a system. She admits her displeasure with how ridiculous this all is and even laughed at how stupid this must look. She reiterates that she cant cancel this order at this point and has tried. However she is gonna just credit me the entire cost of the Iphone and send it free. Even going as far as to sends case and screen protectors. She asks that I please call in the morning using Dana's direct line and have her deal with calling UPS to stop the shipment when they get it. She says that she'll not be working for 2 days but will make sure that its all dealt with when shes back to be sure there are no problems. She says to also hold my note 7 as collateral until they send me a note 7 in the future which they should call about in the coming weeks.  I thank her and finally set down my phone. 
 Its 1am and I have two 800 dollar iphones, case, and screen protectors coming and it only costed me about 7 hours of calls and sitting in the store, a few gallons of gas, and about 98% of my patience. 
 Morning comes and I call Dana's line as soon as she is supposed to be on duty as I have her hours for the next few days written down. No pickup. I call a few times over the next couple hours and finally decide to just call the note 7 hotline again and the rep sees the note on my account and says she will deal with UPS. 
 So that's it not too bad right? I hope my slightly ticked demeanor is understood but this was the craziest experience in recalls I have ever dealt with. Worse than car recalls where I have had family get free cars worth over 20k once all was said and done. I write this to vent and also get the word out that there is a clear problem at T-Mobile that hopefully Kendall gets the word out about. I just want to make sure no one else deals with this and has better experiences. 
 My final words are gonna be some lessons learned about this process: 
 
 DO NOT LET ANYONE HAVE YOUR NOTE 7 wait until you have the new one confirmed being shipped to you or are being handed it in the store. 
 
 Do not go into the store they can NOT help you and dont become upset with them for this as they simply lack the system to do so. 
 
 Lastly document everything. Who you speak with. Where you go. Whats happening even. Its the best way to cover yourself as this process is being developed. 
 
 
 I now am just waiting for my Iphone and hoping that it all works out and I dont end up getting charged anything after this all but I'm sure this story will only get crazier when its time to get my  replacement. We shall see. 
 Thanks for your time.

prompt_text:

You're a professional wordsmith. Summarize the following blog article into a concise summary, ensuring that all essential information is included. 
[Text Start]: 
So, little background, I've been playing since closed Beta, mostly FTP player (bought the Adventures + 1 Arena in Beta for the golden Legendary), and because of that, I gravitated toward Arena because it was the best way to enjoy all the cards of the game I couldn't craft.  Even though I now have every card in the game, I still enjoy playing arena more than constructed.  I average about 6.5 wins/run and 140ish gold/run, so I'm basically infinite since I play 1 run a day, and quest gold kicks me over 150/day.  I often watch Arena streams and pay attention to Arena threads, and one common theme that's agreed upon in Arena is that Warrior sucks.  If you go to any site that tracks Arena win rates, Warriors are always at the bottom in win rates and percent picked.  Pretty much every Arena streamer agrees that Warrior is far and away the worst class.  Not that there aren't strong cards, but more that many of the cards don't lend themselves well to the Arena format.  With the new expansion soon to be released, I figured I'd analyze the class and everything about it to point out the many flaws of the class, and what I would want as cards to deal with these flaws. 
 Warning: Long 
 
 The Arena Meta 
 
 To understand why Warriors are bad in Arena, you have to understand Arena itself.  In Constructed, decks are built from the ground up to synergize with each other.  This is what makes combo decks or slower decks viable.  Control and Patron Warrior are two examples of it, with Patron Warrior being arguably the most synergistic deck in Hearthstone, and Control Warrior relying on cheap removal and a copious amount of life gain, plus complete board wipes like Brawl, to get to the late game where it drops down big minion after big minion to the point it just overpowers other decks.  In Arena, these decks are impossible to create reliably.  While good players draft for synergy, its impossible to have the synergy required for constructed decks. 
 As a result, Arena is primarily about Tempo and Value over the combo synergy in constructed.  The best cards to draft in Arena are cards that are very strong for their mana cost, which have the ability to gain value by either trading well and killing two or more cards by being played (a 2 for 1), or cards that can "trade up", allowing you to cheat tempo by using a 1 or 2 mana creature to kill a three or four mana creature.  A card like Piloted Shredder, for instance, can often kill one creature by itself, then it spawns another body which can then kill another creature, gaining a 2 for 1 value.  A card like Dark Iron Dwarf allows you to use your cheaper creatures to kill more expensive creatures, thus making your board state stronger than the opponent.  Flamestrike, the most hated card in Arena due to how often you can't play around it, often will kill 4 or 5 cards for 1 card, creating a huge value swing and allowing the Mage class to win through superior card value. 
 Ultimately, the Warrior class cards for the most part fails to have these kinds of cards.  Warriors have many cards which all have a strong synergy with each other, arguably more synergy than any other class in constructed, but in Arena where this synergy is unreliable, you will often end up with inferior decks, that will very easily lose to other decks.  While the Warrior class certainly has strong cards, the vast majority of Warrior cards are heavily situational.  This hurts because, as arena is based on tempo, if I can not use my mana to do something to the board, and the opponent can, I will often lose the game.  Having situational cards that are often dead cards makes this much more likely to happen.  That many of these cards even when they can be used properly will not cause two for one trades makes them that much worse.  Even the Warrior hero power is inferior to all other classes' hero power in arena, which exacerbates their weakness in the format.  The rest of this post will describe just how exactly the Warrior class has problems generating value or tempo from its cards and hero power, and what I feel are the best steps to take in future card releases to fix this problem.. 
 
 The Hero Power 
 
 Blizzard initially created the hero powers to be something that players could do with their excess mana, as well as ways to define each class.  Of all classes in Arena, Warrior has unquestionably the worst hero power in the game (+2 armor), by a large, large margin.  This is because their hero power is almost completely irrelevant to what happens in the game.  Any time a Warrior has to hero power, it is going to put them behind further, compared to other class.  Analyzing the other classes: 
 Two classes add minions to the board (Paladin, Shaman).  Three classes (Druid, Mage, Rogue) have hero powers that deal damage to the board.  Impacting the board in any way contributes to board control, which is more than Armor does. 
 Warlock uses its hero power to draw cards.  The more cards you have, the more you can put on the board, and the more answers you have to the opponent's minions. 
 Priest has a similar hero power to warrior, but they can also heal minions, which is much more valuable than the ability to go over 30 health (which is almost never relevant in Arena), or the ability to Shield Slam (more later).  This often lets priests in the mid to late game make two or more for one trades with their cards, allowing the Priest to gain a card advantage over other classes. 
 Hunter's hero power is the only one outside of warrior which doesn't actually impact the board state, but it is more valuable as a clock for how long the game goes.  The Hunter hero power makes games shorter, while the Warrior hero power makes games last longer.  With no board, a Hunter can still win the game, while with no board, a Warrior will only delay the game longer until they lose or possibly come back. 
 How to fix this: There should be more cards where Armor matters.  As of right now, there are two cards in the game which the hero power can impact: One is Shield Slam, a 1 mana epic which deals minion damage based on the armor you have, but due to a lack of armor synergy in Arena, its effectively a drain life 99% of the time.  The other is Siege Engine, a 5 mana rare 5/5 which gains 1 attack each time you gain armor.  Both of these cards are mediocre in Arena, because the main cards which generate armor are generally not all that good as its hard to get the right synergy to use them right, and the effects are not that powerful.  Shield Slam is usually a Drain Life when it gets used, which is pretty poor vaue.  Also, by being an Epic and Rare card respectively, it means that its that much harder for the hero power to get value.  There are other cards that rely on health instead of armor for triggers, but they can be ignored for Arena, even the class cards. 
 To get value out of the hero power, you need more cards which impact the board when you use your hero power.  As you need to keep constructed in mind, any card that uses total armor would be a bad idea due to how absurdly high constructed armor can get, and how low arena armor usually is.  I think the best option would be to make a Warrior version of Shadowboxer or Flamewaker, dependent on when you gain armor.  I'd say a 2-4 mana minion that deals 1 random damage to an enemy minion every time you gain armor.  The mid-ranged ping effect would be useful in coming back from behind, or setting up an execute if you have the card. 
 
 Warrior Spells 
 
 Anyone who has played Warrior in constructed, Control or Patron, knows how well Warriors can have spells synergize with each other.  The problem is, as Arena is much more tempo and minion based, and because you can only build your deck on what you get, that often you will get spells or pieces that don't have good synergy, or are stuck in your hand as you wait to get the pieces together to make full use out of the Spells.  If you choose to take many of the Warrior spells, there's a good chance it'll either be a dead card for most of the game, or an ok card that really isn't worth the card slot, or gains card or tempo value.  Going over the various Warrior spells, from good to bad: 
 Execute, Slam, Cleave: Awesome spells, real high value for their mana costs. 
 Battle Rage, Commanding Shout: Good spells, if you have the right board they win games, but at their worst they're not that bad of cards.  Often cards you want to hold for the right play, so situational in spite of their upside. 
 Brawl: Special tier by itself, its a dead card unless the opponent plays into it, and is only useful if you're behind on board.  It either wins you games or sits in your hand the entire game. 
 Upgrade, Inner Rage, Revenge, Whirlwind, Rampage: Situational cards that are sometimes useful but aren't really high enough impact to be worth a card slot, or where its difficult to get the card combos to work. 
 Mortal Strike, Shield Block, Shield Slam, Heroic Strike: Card that are really not all that powerful.  Special mention to Heroic Strike in that, it is good damage for mana, but because you always want a weapon, its often overkill, which is why I slot it here. 
 Bouncing Blades, Charge: Bad cards, will rarely work as they should. 
 So, of spells, Warrior has (IMO) 3 great, 2 good, one super high variance, 5 ok to poor, 4 bad, 2 very bad. 
 How to fix this: Blizzard apparently already knew about this problem, because many of the Warrior spells have their effects on other cards.  Inner Rage on Cruel Taskmaster, Whirlwind on Death's Bite, along with Dread Infernal and Unstable Ghoul for non-warrior cards, and Shield Block's armor on Shield Maiden.  Warrior minions which gave you the Rampage or Upgrade effects would be nice so you could get those effects, but the spells are always going to be options to draft, and will always drag down your drafts because they'll take up options from better cards.   There is really no way to fix that issue. 
 My best thought on how to address the issue of warrior spells being poor would be to add a "Mad Scientist" card for warriors, which draws specifically Warrior spells from your deck into the hand.  In this case, you could deal with the situational nature of the cards by having them in your hand, so if they are dead you can still have other cards to play.  The best Warrior runs I've had were runs where I had a lot of card draw to be able to play a lowish mana tempo game and not run out of steam, so more card draw for Warriors would help them.  This would obviously be very powerful in constructed, but I'm not sure if it'd be good enough in Patron/Control warrior to justify a card slot. 
 
 Warrior Minions 
 
 I would argue that, from a minion quality perspective, Warrior has the weakest selection of minions in the game.  Every class except for Druid has a common or rare minion that either is very hard to remove off the board efficiently (Imp Gang Boss, Minibot, Highmane), has a strong impact on the board when its played (Fire Elemental, Goblin Autobarber, Aldor Peacekeeper), or has absurdly strong stats for its cost (Water Elemental, Dark Cultist, Fireguard Destroyer).  Warrior has two cards that can be game winning, but they are dependent a lot on the board state, and aren't that difficult to remove.  Again, going over the cards: 
 Frothing Berserker, Warsong Commander: Lumped in cause they can win games by themselves as any constructed player knows, although in different ways.  They're both cards you need to protect to get real strong value out of though. 
 Cruel Taskmaster: Tier by itself, its a good card cause its versatile, but its either a worse Abusive Sergeant, or a better Elven Archer.  Its a 2 drop you never want to play on 2 even if useful. 
 Korkron Elite: Also by itself, a 4/3  with charge for 4 is ok, its not bad, but its only really good when going face.  3 health on 4 is underwhelming, 4 damage removal on 4 is underwhelming, and it feels wasted trying to get a 2 for 1 value by killing a small minion. 
 Shieldmaiden, Siege Engine, Warbot: Two ok minions and one minion that never works and ruins topdecks, that are inferior to the higher tiered 1/5/6 drops you'd get from neutral cards.  Again, class cards that are worse than at least 3 other neutral common minions. 
 Armorsmith, Screwjank Clunker, Axe Flinger: Bad stats on the cards for their mana cost.  Axe Flinger makes me think Blizzard wants Warrior to suck in Arena because, I do not think there's any way, shape, or form a 3/5 Axe Flinger is broken or any more broken than what goes on anyways in constructed.  Screwjank would be better if it had Houndmaster stats because then it could do more damage and trade better, but at 2/5  just doesn't clear enough to be useful. 
 How to fix this: Well to start, make Axe Flinger a 3/5, but Blizzard won't do that.  Warrior needs a stand alone minion that is very OP and can anchor their early game.  They need their own version of Minibot or Imp Gang Boss or Animal Companion.  In the other sections, I mentioned my ideas for a Warrior version of Flamewaker or Shadowboxer, or for more warrior minions like Cruel Taskmaster which incorporate Warrior spells into the minion to get value of of strong cards that just are too situational or not strong enough to justify a deck spot. 
 In addition to these cards, other useful cards would be cards that either stall out the game, or deal AoE ping damage (like Foe Reaper 9000) would be really useful for early game board control and coming back from poor starts.  Random ideas I had were a 3 mana 1/5 or 2/4 taunt, every time a minion attacks this minion, deal 1 additional damage to it.  It would be basically a 2/5 or 3/4 taunt, with added upside, which would not be game-breaking in constructed, and slow down Arena for Warriors to parlay their Value edge.  Additionally, if you wanted to make it super-strong, you could make it deal 1 damage before a minion attacks into it, which would clear off divine shields/prevent minions with 1 HP from attacking it, but I think that effect might be so strong Blizzard would stat it as a 2/3, which would suck and make it worthless. 
 Another one would be either a 4 mana 2/4 or 5 mana 3/5 with charge, and dealing 1 damage to adjacent minions on attack.  A little slower, but a way for Warriors to come back in the mid-game and set up executes or easier weapon clears, while again not being game-breaking in constructed.  As another taunt idea, a 4-6 mana creature that deals 1 damage to all other characters every time it takes damage would be another nice control card for Warriors, plus the ability proc Enrage effects easier. 
 
 Warrior Weapons 
 
 The class defining feature of Warriors.  Warrior has the most value-efficient weapons in the game, and often an entire Arena run for Warriors is predicated on if they draft weapons, and if they draw their weapons on the right turn.  There is a reason that Fiery War Axe is commonly called Fiery Win Axe, and that's because if you get it in your opening hand, you generally kill two of your opponent's minions for one, and that early game value edge will win you games similar to Minibot killing multiple minions.  Gorehowl may be the best value card in the game, Death's Bite is very strong due to its deathrattle, Arcanite Reaper is a 2 turn pyroblast for half the cost, and Arathi Weaponsmith allows you to put a minion on the board while getting rid of pesky little creatures to truly control the board.  All of the Warrior weapons are great.  All 5 of them.  The weapons were so strong that pre-GvG, while Warrior was not the best class, it was certainly a good class in Arena and not dreadful to pick.  So, what happened when GvG came out? 
 Piloted Shredder happened.  Annoy-o-tron happened.  Shielded Minibot happened.  Coghammer happened.  Snowchugger happened.  Spider Tank and Ogre Brute happened.  Even Gilblin Stalker happened.  Then Imp Gang Boss happened in BRM.  In short, GvG improved the minion quality so much that having an early-game War Axe or Death's Bite wasn't strong enough to clear these minions, meaning the tempo Warriors needed wasn't there. 
 On top of this, Warriors have gotten nothing in GvG or BRM.  Every other class except Druid got a great card from BRM which made them vastly stronger in Arena, and Warriors got crap.  Every class got at least something cool in BRM, and Warriors got crap outside of the occasional Patron, which if you've ever done Patron Warrior in Arena, you know that it just doesn't work, because its not consistent enough to get the combos off and not have dead cards. 
 This doesn't account for the one major problem with weapons: Having too many of them.  As a Warrior, your best cards are weapons, and you pretty much need to always have one equipped or ready to equip to keep control of the board.  However, once you get to 5-7 weapons, you get to the point where you will have games where your hand is full of good weapons you can't use.  If I draft 4 mini-bots as a Paladin, I can put down a minibot if I already have one in play.  If I draft 4 War Axes, and I get 3 in my opening hand, I'm probably skipping a turn and losing the game cause of that.  So, even the real strong value cards of Warriors have drawbacks attached to them. 
 How to fix this: Any card that summons/buffs weapons would obviously be useful to Warriors and make them more consistent.  Unstable Weaponsmith as a spell would be interesting to get a turn 4 Gorehowl, although this might be too strong since there are very few really bad weapons.  (Ogre Warmaul does not exist)  Warrior itself doesn't necessarily need more weapons, but because of how valuable the weapons are to the class, more options to get weapons would really help the class for Arena stability. 
 While deathrattle and higher health minions serve to make the game more about minion trading and less about removal, due to Warrior's weakness, a powerful silence effect would be very useful to dealing with the deathrattle creatures that screw up Weapon's removal ability.  I would love to see the Shattering Throw ability come into Hearthstone, best as a 3 mana spell to Silence, then deal 3 damage to an enemy minion.  Its an upscaled Earth Shock, but it would be very, very strong in the early game.  It'd deal with Harvest Golem and Scarlet Crusader for the same value, trade up against Piloted Shredder, trade down against Minibot and Annoy-o-tron but still be worthwhile, and set up weapon kills on bigger minions like Sludge Belcher.  Plus, it'd be a tiny bit of spell damage to deal with minions like Zap-o-matic or Flesheating Ghoul or Questing Adventuer or Micro Machine that, if protected by taunts, flat out win games with little interaction. 
 The only way I can see dealing with the glut of weapons is to find more ways to get use out of weapons.  Giving warriors a Hellfire/Bladefury like effect, to destroy your weapon and deal that damage to all minions, would be a strong AoE for Warriors, maybe a little too similar to brawl, but would give Warriors a board clearing AOE they need to come back if they start slow.  Another idea would be a spell to give Warriors Windfury for one turn.  If you set this at 3 mana, it would be a real strong removal tool, while at the same time not being that OP for Warriors, and justify having more weapons since you could get rid of them in one turn.  With a Fiery War Axe, you're paying 3 mana for 3 damage: Death's Bite is 3 mana for a swipe which hits the whole board, and Arcanite is 3 mana for a Kill Command.  It wouldn't be that OP for OTK weapon builds when you consider that Shaman has access to Windfury already (Spell + Doomhammer), plus a better buff option in Rockbiter Weapon.

theoretical studies of electronic structure of high - energy - density plasmas are of great interest for the understanding of radiative transfer and equation of state ( eos ) and for the simulation of laser - driven experiments .
such investigations play a major role in astrophysics and inertial confinement fusion .
the present work consists in a theoretical study of atomic physics of ions in plasmas taking screening effects into account .
it is essential , in order to describe dense plasmas and especially their ability to absorb electromagnetic radiations , to characterize ions in the most realistic way , through a consistent thermodynamic modeling .
photo - absorption calculations using self - consistent `` detailed - term accounting '' ( dta ) or `` detailed - configuration accounting '' ( dca ) have been performed ( see for instance goldberg _

all ionic species are treated in all their physically realistic configurations .
however , the number of relevant configurations in a plasma can be really huge , especially for high values of atomic number @xmath0 , and all of them can not be taken into account . indeed , requiring that each configuration has its own basis of one - electron wavefunctions and including configuration mixing leads to a high numerical cost .
the superconfiguration method has been invented @xcite in order to overcome this problem in an approximate way and to provide more accurate results than average - atom models .
this approach includes relaxation effects ( different basis of wavefunctions for the upper and lower states involved in a transition ) , and allows inclusion of configuration interaction between relativistic sub - configurations of a non - relativistic configuration @xcite .
as a configuration is defined by shells occupied by an integer number of bound electrons , a superconfiguration ( sc ) is defined by supershells , which are groups of shells close in energy @xcite ( _ i.e. _ whose energies differ from less than @xmath1 ) .

equation of state of dense matter can be addressed by several techniques such as , for instance , chemical - picture models , quantum - molecular dynamics , path - integral monte carlo , or average - atom models .
the latest are particularly well suited for high - z elements , and hot dense plasmas with coupling parameter @xmath18 , namely strongly correlated plasmas .
the model presented here is close to aa models , but constitutes an attempt to include better ( less averaged ) atomic physics . for each sc ,
bound electrons are treated quantum mechanically and free electrons within the thomas - fermi ( tf ) approximation ( hybrid model ) .
once their electronic structure has been calculated , scs of the same charge can be grouped into ions . at this stage ,
the plasma can be considered as an ensemble of ions , containing bound electrons , and immersed in a free - electron gas .
it was shown @xcite that , provided that ions of different charges have different volumes , the electronic pressure , calculated together with ionic volumes in a self - consistent way , must be equal for each ion .
the improvement in thermodynamic consistency brought by the diversity of ionic volumes ( in other words the `` redefinition '' of ions ) encourage us to apply this approach to eos calculations .
the purpose of the work presented in @xcite was to propose a method for the treatment of mixtures , and the issue of thermodynamic consistency was not addressed . in the present work ,
we focus on the expression of pressure , and especially on the proper form of the quantum virial theorem .
it is shown that the universal form of the virial theorem for a quantum - statistical model ( _ i.e. _ a virial theorem that does not depend on the boundary conditions of the wavefunctions ) is different from the one proposed in @xcite , which relies in an intrinsic way on neumann or dirichlet conditions .
moreover , we find that the pressure obtained from the generalized virial theorem presented here is equal to the stress - tensor formula proposed in @xcite and can be obtained by minimization of the free energy .
such a formula can be also applied to free - electrons @xcite , but for a sake of simplicity we consider here the `` hybrid '' model , in which free electrons are treated semi - classically .
the transformation of an electron state from being bound to being a part of the continuum is gradual @xcite .
however , although the hybrid model provides an accurate description of strongly correlated plasmas , the confinement of an ion in a finite volume may still lead , in our model and when the matter density is sufficiently high , to unacceptable discontinuities in the thermodynamic functions when a bound level disappears ( pressure ionization ) . such discontinuities in thermodynamic functions are due to the fact that it is difficult to obtain a variational formulation of the problem .    our eos model relying on a self - consistent - field calculation of screened scs with tf free electrons and quantum bound electrons

prompt_text:
You're a professional wordsmith. Summarize the following report into a concise summary, ensuring that all essential information is included. 
[Text Start]: 
Letter
Businesses of any size can be unsuspecting victims of tax fraud  schemes, including business identity theft refund fraud (business IDT).  According to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), business IDT occurs  when thieves create, use, or try to use a business’s identifying  information—such as an Employer Identification Number (EIN)—in an  attempt to claim a tax refund.
IRS has recognized business IDT as a growing threat. IRS has reported  that identity thieves show a sophisticated knowledge of the tax code and  filing practices as they attempt to obtain valuable data that enable them to  file fraudulent returns with potentially large refunds. In April 2019, IRS  reported a 10 percent increase in the number of businesses notifying IRS  that they have been victims of business IDT (2,233 notifications in 2017 to  2,450 in 2018). In addition to costing the government money, business  IDT can hurt a business’s reputation and credit and make a business  more susceptible to other types of financial fraud.
IRS has noted that both businesses and individuals can suffer significant  financial, social, and emotional hardship as victims of identity theft (IDT)  refund fraud. As we have reported previously, the risk of IDT refund fraud  has increased as personally identifiable information (PII) has become  more readily available through cyberattacks and data breaches.  Businesses are further at risk of IDT refund fraud because their  information is often easy to obtain, as they may post key information  online, such as the names of corporate officers, address, and number of  employees. Additional business information can also be obtained through  online commercial databases. Further, federal regulations require some  types of businesses to file public reports that include data which could be  useful to a fraudster, such as data from annual financial statements. The  availability of both PII and business information poses a threat to the tax  system, making it more difficult for IRS to distinguish legitimate taxpayers  from fraudsters.
Within this context, you asked us to examine IRS’s efforts to detect,  prevent, and resolve business IDT. This report (1) describes IRS’s efforts  to detect business IDT, (2) evaluates the extent to which IRS’s efforts to  prevent business IDT are consistent with selected fraud risk management  leading practices, and (3) assesses IRS’s efforts to resolve business IDT  cases.
To address all of our objectives, we reviewed our prior reports on  individual IDT refund fraud and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax  Administration’s (TIGTA) prior reports on business IDT. We also  interviewed IRS officials from business units responsible for detecting,  preventing, and resolving business IDT cases, specifically from Return  Integrity and Compliance Services (RICS), Accounts Management (AM),  and Criminal Investigation (CI). In December 2018, we visited IRS’s  campus in Ogden, Utah, to interview officials responsible for IRS’s  business IDT efforts and to observe how RICS and AM staff process and  research business IDT cases using IRS information technology systems  and tools.
To describe IRS’s current efforts to detect business IDT refund fraud, we  reviewed documentation describing the business IDT fraud filters IRS  implemented from 2017 through 2019. We also analyzed data from IRS’s  Dependent Database (DDb) on business IDT fraud filter results, and data  from the Business Master File Identity Check (BMFIC) case management  system for applicable returns IRS received from mid-January 2017  through mid-August 2019. This was the most recent, complete, and  available set of data at the time of our review. We tested key data  elements, including computerized checks for missing, out-of-range, or  logically inaccurate data, and interviewed officials knowledgeable about  the data to discuss any limitations.
We determined that these data were sufficiently reliable to describe the  volume of incoming returns stopped by business IDT fraud filters,  associated refunds, and the outcome of business IDT cases. We also  reviewed documentation and interviewed officials to understand IRS’s  efforts to collaborate with external partners to detect and prevent  business IDT.
To evaluate the extent to which IRS’s efforts to prevent business IDT are  consistent with selected fraud risk management leading practices, we  reviewed the Fraud Reduction and Data Analytics Act of 2015 (FRDAA)  and A Framework for Managing Fraud Risks in Federal Programs (Fraud  Risk Framework). We generally focused our review on the first two  components of the Fraud Risk Framework: (1) commit to combating fraud  by creating an organizational culture and structure conducive to fraud risk  management, and (2) plan regular fraud risk assessments and assess  risks to determine a fraud risk profile. In doing so, we reviewed agency  strategic planning documents, organizational charts, and interviewed IRS  officials to understand each business unit’s respective role in detecting,  preventing, and resolving business IDT.
We reviewed documentation on IRS’s efforts to identify and assess  business IDT fraud risks, relevant Internal Revenue Manual (IRM)  sections, and prior GAO, TIGTA, and National Taxpayer Advocate reports  related to three inherent fraud risks to business IDT. Additionally, we  obtained information from interviews with RICS, AM, CI, RAAS, and IRS’s  Office of the Chief Risk Officer to understand IRS’s efforts to combat  business IDT through fraud risk management. We also reviewed  documents and information on IRS’s efforts to collect quality data on  incoming business and employment returns. We compared these efforts  to Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government related to  using quality information and leading practices identified in the Fraud Risk  Framework.
To assess IRS’s current efforts to resolve business IDT cases, we  reviewed IRS procedures for managing, researching, and resolving  business IDT cases. We analyzed data from BMFIC and IRS’s  Correspondence Imaging System (CIS) to determine how long RICS and  AM took to resolve business IDT cases. We assessed the reliability of  CIS data by testing key data elements and interviewing knowledgeable  IRS officials. Based on this effort and our assessment of BMFIC data  reliability described above, we determined that these data were  sufficiently reliable to determine how long it took RICS and AM to resolve  business IDT cases.
We also interviewed IRS officials to determine potential reasons for  delays in resolving cases. Finally, we compared RICS and AM’s efforts to  resolve business IDT cases against Office of Management and Budget  (OMB) guidance on program management and providing customer  service. See appendix I for details on our scope and methodology.
We conducted this performance audit from July 2018 to January 2020 in  accordance with generally accepted government auditing standards.  Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain  sufficient, appropriate evidence to provide a reasonable basis for our  findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. We believe that  the evidence obtained provides a reasonable basis for our findings and  conclusions based on our audit objectives.
Appendix I: Objectives, Scope, and Methodology
Our objectives were to (1) describe the Internal Revenue Service’s (IRS)  efforts to detect business identity theft refund fraud (business IDT), (2)  evaluate the extent to which IRS’s efforts to prevent business IDT are  consistent with selected fraud risk management leading practices, and (3)  assess IRS’s efforts to resolve business IDT cases. In this report,  business IDT refers to the fraudulent use of both business and  employment tax forms. Both of these types of forms require an Employer  Identification Number (EIN) when filing with IRS, and a fraudster can file  these forms to obtain a refund.
To address all of our objectives, we reviewed our prior reports on  individual identity theft refund fraud and the Treasury Inspector General  for Tax Administration’s (TIGTA) prior reports on business IDT. We also  interviewed IRS officials from business units responsible for detecting,  preventing, and resolving business IDT cases, specifically from Return  Integrity and Compliance Services (RICS), Accounts Management (AM),  and Criminal Investigation (CI). In December 2018, we visited IRS’s  campus in Ogden, Utah, to interview officials responsible for IRS’s  business IDT efforts and to observe how RICS and AM staff process and  research business IDT cases using IRS information technology systems  and tools.
To describe IRS’s current processes to detect business IDT refund fraud,  we reviewed documentation describing the business IDT fraud filters IRS  implemented from 2017 through 2019, including the logic for each filter  and the forms to which they apply. In addition, we analyzed data from  IRS’s Dependent Database (DDb) on business IDT fraud filter results for  applicable incoming business and employment tax returns IRS received  from mid-January 2017 through mid-August 2019. This was the most  recent, complete, and available set of data at the time of our review. This  analysis showed the volume of returns selected by IRS’s business IDT  fraud filters by form, tax processing year, and associated refund amount.
We also analyzed data from IRS’s Business Master File Identity Check  (BMFIC) system—RICS’s case management system for business IDT  returns flagged by DDb—for cases opened from mid-January 2017  through mid-August 2019. These were the most complete set of data  available at the time of our review. Our analysis of BMFIC data showed  the number of returns that RICS researched as potential business IDT,  the outcome of the case, and associated refund amounts. For the  purpose of analysis and reporting, we grouped business IDT case  outcomes into three categories: confirmed business IDT, not business  IDT, and open/unresolved.
We assessed the reliability of data from these systems by: (1) testing key  data elements, including checks for missing, out-of-range, or logically  inaccurate data; (2) reviewing documents for information about the data  and IRS’s systems; and (3) interviewing officials knowledgeable about the  data to discuss any limitations. We determined that these data were  sufficiently reliable to describe the volume of incoming returns stopped by  business IDT fraud filters, associated refunds, and the outcome of  business IDT cases.
To understand IRS’s efforts to collaborate with external partners to detect  and prevent business IDT, we interviewed IRS and state officials from the  Security Summit’s Business IDT sub-workgroup and reviewed IRS’s 2018  report which analyzed business-related data elements from incoming tax  returns. We also interviewed IRS officials about a pilot program with the  Alabama Department of Labor to help detect and deactivate potentially  suspicious EINs established in that state. For context, we obtained  information from January to December 2018 from IRS on the  performance of this pilot, including the number of EINs identified as  fraudulent.
To evaluate the extent to which IRS’s efforts to prevent business IDT are  consistent with selected fraud risk management leading practices, we  reviewed the Fraud Reduction and Data Analytics Act (FRDAA) of 2015  and leading practices outlined in A Framework for Managing Fraud Risks  in Federal Programs (Fraud Risk Framework). We generally focused our  review on the first two components of the Fraud Risk Framework: (1)  commit to combating fraud by creating an organizational culture and  structure conducive to fraud risk management, and (2) plan regular fraud  risk assessments and assess risks to determine a fraud risk profile. We  reviewed agency documents and information obtained from interviews, as  described below, and compared them against leading practices identified  in the Fraud Risk Framework related to these two components.
We reviewed IRS’s most recent strategic planning documents related  to reducing fraud, IRS organizational charts, and relevant Internal  Revenue Manual (IRM) sections on business IDT operations and  procedures. We interviewed officials from RICS, AM, CI, and the  Office of Research, Applied Analytics, and Statistics (RAAS) to  understand each business unit’s respective role in detecting,  preventing, and resolving business IDT cases and the extent to which  business units work together on day-to-day and longer-term efforts. In  addition, we reviewed IRS reports on business IDT case workload.  We also reviewed meeting notes from IRS’s IDT Executive Steering  Committee (July and October 2017, and January and October 2018)  to understand the extent to which IRS’s executive-level groups are, for  example, involved in helping guide business IDT efforts or made  aware of business IDT challenges.
We interviewed officials from RICS, AM, CI, and RAAS and reviewed  documentation on IRS’s efforts to identify and assess business IDT  fraud risks. These included reviewing RAAS’s analyses on business  IDT fraud filter performance, descriptions of potential new fraud filters  that IRS may implement in the future, and the Wage and Investment  Division’s risk register. We also interviewed officials from IRS’s Office  of the Chief Risk Officer to understand IRS’s efforts to compile and  report on enterprise-wide fraud risks and agency efforts to develop an  antifraud culture.
Further, we reviewed documentation related to three inherent fraud  risks to business IDT that we identified in the course of our work:  correspondence-based authentication, EIN vulnerabilities, and high  false-detection rates for IDT fraud filters. This included reviewing  prior GAO, TIGTA, and National Taxpayer Advocate reports and the  status of open recommendations, and relevant IRM sections. We  reviewed the methodologies of these reports and found them  reasonable for the purpose of describing the inherent risks related to  business IDT.
In addition, we identified a false detection rate for business IDT fraud  filters based on BMFIC cases opened from mid-January 2017 through  December 2018. To do so, we compared the number of cases IRS  determined were not business IDT, relative to the total number of  cases. We did not include BMFIC cases from 2019 because at the  time of our analysis, about 27 percent of those cases were  unresolved.
We also assessed the extent to which IRS is positioned to estimate  the size and scope of business IDT. To do so, we reviewed  documents and information on IRS’s efforts to collect quality data on  incoming business and employment returns. We compared these  efforts to leading practices associated with the first two components of  the Fraud Risk Framework and Standards for Internal Control in the  Federal Government related to using quality information.  Specifically, we determined what proportion of incoming business and  employment tax forms filed in 2018 would have been screened by  business IDT fraud filters, by tax form type. We also reviewed a  preliminary plan and interviewed RAAS and RICS officials on their  efforts to develop a business IDT taxonomy.
To assess IRS’s efforts to resolve business IDT cases, we reviewed IRS  procedures for managing, researching, and resolving pre-refund and  post-refund business IDT cases. We interviewed officials from RICS and  AM to understand the rationale behind their respective current case  resolution time frames, and potential reasons for case resolution delays.  We compared RICS and AM’s efforts to resolve business IDT cases  against Office of Management and Budget guidance on program  management and providing customer service. To determine RICS’s  performance in resolving business IDT cases identified during the pre- refund phase, we analyzed 181,032 cases from BMFIC, described above.
Specifically, we calculated the duration between when RICS opened the  case in BMFIC to when the case was closed. In addition, we determined  how many cases in RICS’s inventory were open at the time of our  analysis in August 2019. For these open cases, we manually added the  date we received the data as the date the case was closed. This was an  indicator of the minimum amount of time RICS could have taken to close  these cases.
For this analysis, we did not include cases opened and closed in 2019  because we wanted to ensure there was sufficient time for RICS to  research and close a case. We determined that cases opened by the end  of December 2018 gave both RICS and AM (discussed below) enough  time to resolve a case. In addition, we identified an anomaly in RICS’s  2019 cases. IRS officials stated that a new fraud filter inaccurately  flagged incoming returns on one form, and IRS released these returns.  Our analysis of RICS’s data showed that these returns accounted for  about 65 percent of closed cases in 2019, and that they were resolved in  an unusually short time frame (fewer than 45 days) thus skewing the  overall data. We also did not include 1,679 cases that were opened and  closed in zero or fewer days.
To determine AM’s performance in resolving business IDT cases  identified during the post-refund phase, we analyzed 1,997 relevant  business IDT cases from IRS’s Correspondence Imaging System (CIS)  that AM opened from July 2016 through December 2018. As discussed  earlier, we did not include cases opened and closed in 2019 to allow AM  enough time to research and resolve a case. We calculated the duration  between when AM opened the case in CIS to when the case was closed.  We also determined how many cases in AM’s inventory were open at the  time of our analysis. For these open cases, we manually added the date  we received the data as the date the case was closed. This was an  indicator of the minimum amount of time AM could have taken to close  these cases. We assessed the reliability of the CIS data by reviewing  relevant documents, testing key data elements, and interviewing  knowledgeable IRS officials. We determined that the data from CIS was  sufficiently reliable to determine how long it took AM to resolve post- refund business IDT cases during this time period.
We conducted this performance audit from July 2018 to January 2020 in  accordance with generally accepted government auditing standards.  Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain  sufficient, appropriate evidence to provide a reasonable basis for our  findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. We believe that  the evidence obtained provides a reasonable basis for our findings and  conclusions based on our audit objectives.
Appendix II: Comments from the Internal Revenue Service
Appendix III: GAO Contact and Acknowledgments
